newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Illovo keeps Lonrho non-sugar units for now.
newsitem.headline: Illovo keeps Lonrho non-sugar units for now.

text.p: South Africa's Illovo Sugar Ltd would not immediately sell off the non-sugar interests held by Lonrho Sugar Corp Ltd, which it took over on Thursday, Illovo's managing director Don MacLeod said on Friday.

Commenting on speculation that Illovo might sell the hotel interests of Lonhro's Mauritius-listed company Mon Tresor Mon Desert (MTMD), and possibly even sell its whole Mauritius operation, MacLeod said investors would first be consulted.

"(Lonrho) is a listed company and it does have a whole mix of assets. We have got to look at that mix of assets in terms of how various investors feel that the thing should be maintained as regards the sort of returns they would like to get from their overall investment," he told a news conference.
"We are certainly going to assess what there is with the business on the basis that we are going to remain focused on what we are involved in. Sugar and downstream products, that's our business."
Illovo, which has a 44 percent domestic market share, has become Afica's largest sugar group after the deal and will be one of the world's lowest-cost sugar producers.
With 15 mills in five southern African countries, MacLeod predicted they could produce 1.8 million tonnes of sugar in the next two years.
Although further expansion into Africa would be put on hold for now following the 1.6 billion rand acquisition of Lonhro Plc's sugar division, opportunities would again be sought in the future.
The Lonrho unit has operations in South Africa, Malawi, Swaziland and Mauritius.
"This is a pretty big acquisition and we need to digest everything before we rush off anywhere else...but in the longer term we will continue to look at opportunities in Africa" he said.

He said the 12-member Southern African Development Community (SADC) should draw up a sugar protocol for the future to develop the industry and prevent smaller sugar-producing countries being flooded by their bigger neighbours.

"We believe that both the Southern African Customs Union and SADC have to have a sugar protocol and that we've all got to behave in the right manner so that the developments that can take place in Africa as a whole are able to go forward."
